title: A foolish consistency
hookLine: a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds (Self-Reliance)

cards: "But that's not what you said last year." It lands like a trap. Someone has dug up an old opinion of yours, a post, a remark at dinner, and set it next to what you think now.
The two don't match. The pull is to do one of two things: pretend you never really changed, or defend the old view just to look steady.
Emerson saw that pull clearly, and in Self-Reliance he named it in a line that gets quoted, sometimes with one important word left out. The missing word is the whole lesson.

teach.b: First, the sentence, whole: "A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds, adored by little statesmen and philosophers and divines." The word that keeps getting dropped is foolish.
Emerson isn't against consistency. Keeping a promise is consistent. Showing up for a friend year after year is consistent.

He's against sticking to a position only because you once said it. A hobgoblin is a small mischievous spirit, the kind that haunts a house: a petty little ghost that keeps a mind from moving. Second, why we do it.
We hold on to our past words, Emerson says, because other people have nothing else to judge us by.
They only have the record, so we start living for the record. Third, his remedy.
Speak what you think now in hard words, and tomorrow speak what tomorrow thinks in hard words again, even if it contradicts everything you said today.

You'll be misunderstood, he admits, and answers with a line of his own: "To be great is to be misunderstood." He names people misunderstood in their day, Socrates and Galileo among them. Fourth, what holds it together.
Emerson trusts that a life lived honestly has a deeper shape than any one opinion.
Seen from far enough off, he says, the zigzags of an honest life line up, the way a ship's tacking adds up to a course.
Changing your mind isn't betraying yourself. Sometimes it's the faithful thing to do.

how: Some readers use Emerson's line about a foolish consistency to make room for honest changes of mind, while keeping the steady kind of consistency that keeps promises and friendships.

games.why: speak what you think now in hard words, and tomorrow what tomorrow thinks, even if it contradicts today.

practice: Look for an opinion you've carried mostly out of habit, about a person, a food, a place, a kind of music, something decided once and not looked at since. Turn it over honestly and ask what you actually think today.
If it's the same, fine; if not, let it change, right here, without explaining to anyone.
